en: Heating ice causes its water molecules to gain energy and move faster, breaking their rigid structure to form liquid water.
When liquid water absorbs heat from the sun, its molecules move fast enough to escape into the air as water vapor.
Stirring sugar in hot water breaks the sugar crystals apart, allowing the sugar molecules to spread evenly and form a solution.
Exposing iron to oxygen and moisture causes a chemical reaction that produces a flaky, reddish-brown substance called iron oxide or rust.
Pouring a sand and water mixture through filter paper traps the solid sand particles while allowing the liquid water to pass through.
A solid object floats in water if it is less dense than water, meaning it has less mass for its specific volume.
Heating baking soda causes it to undergo a chemical change, releasing carbon dioxide gas that makes baked goods rise.
Cooling warm water vapor causes its molecules to lose energy and slow down, clustering together to form liquid water droplets.
Removing heat from liquid water causes its molecules to slow down and lock into a fixed, crystalline structure, forming solid ice.
Passing a magnet over a mixture of iron filings and sand attracts the magnetic iron, physically separating it from the non-magnetic sand.
Dropping chalk into vinegar causes an acid-base chemical reaction that produces bubbling carbon dioxide gas and dissolves the solid calcium carbonate.
Touching a metal spoon in hot soup feels hotter than a wooden spoon because metal conducts heat energy to your hand much faster.
